entries.title: The Abbasid Caliphate
entries.year_ce: 750–1258 CE (Baghdad); later shadow caliphate in Cairo under Mamluks
entries.summary: The Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads in 750 CE and built a new caliphate centered on Baghdad, associated with a flourishing of learning, administration, and culture often called the Islamic Golden Age.
entries.detailed_information: Claiming descent from al-Abbas, uncle of the Prophet, the Abbasids shifted the imperial center to Iraq. Baghdad (founded by al-Mansur) became a major world city. The early and middle Abbasid periods saw translation movements, advances in science and philosophy, sophisticated bureaucracy, and rich literature. Over time, real power fragmented among provincial dynasties while the caliph often remained a symbolic figure. The Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258 CE ended the classical Abbasid caliphate in Iraq.
entries.historical_significance: Central dynasty of classical Islamic civilization and learning.

entries.title: Abbasid Golden Age and the House of Wisdom
entries.summary: During the high Abbasid period, scholars in and around Baghdad translated, preserved, and expanded knowledge in medicine, astronomy, mathematics, philosophy, and literature.
entries.detailed_information: Patronage under caliphs such as Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun supported translation from Greek, Persian, and other traditions into Arabic. Institutions and circles associated with the Bayt al-Hikma (House of Wisdom) symbolize this movement, though modern historians debate the exact institutional form of the House of Wisdom. The period produced enduring contributions later transmitted to other regions, including Europe.
entries.historical_significance: Key phase of scientific and intellectual flourishing in Islamic civilization.
entries.disputed_notes: The precise nature and organization of the House of Wisdom is debated by modern historians.

entries.title: Decline and Fall of the Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad
entries.summary: Abbasid political power fragmented over centuries due to provincial dynasties, military interventions, and economic strain. The Mongol conquest of Baghdad in 1258 CE ended the caliphate there.
entries.detailed_information: From the 9th–10th centuries, Turkish military elites, regional dynasties (Buyids, Seljuks, and others), and internal court conflicts reduced caliphal autonomy. The caliph often retained religious prestige while sultans held real power. In 1258, Mongol forces under Hulagu Khan sacked Baghdad, killing the caliph al-Musta'sim and devastating the city. A later Abbasid line existed ceremonially under the Mamluks in Cairo, but the classical Baghdad caliphate was over.
entries.historical_significance: Marks a dramatic end to the classical Abbasid imperial center.

entries.title: How the Abbasids Came to Power
entries.summary: The Abbasids rose through a revolutionary movement based especially in Khurasan, overthrowing the Umayyads in 750 CE and establishing a new caliphal dynasty.
entries.detailed_information: Revolutionary propaganda mobilized discontent against Umayyad rule. Abu Muslim's forces were decisive. After victory, the Abbasids consolidated power in Iraq, eventually founding Baghdad. Early Abbasid politics included eliminating rivals and managing the expectations of diverse supporters.
entries.historical_significance: Dynastic transfer that reshaped Islamic imperial geography and culture.
